articles.title: Is it true that … hard water damages hair?
articles.summary: Mineral deposits can accumulate, making hair drier, but removing them can cause different problems. From hair treatments to shower filters, a wave of products have been launched promising to protect hair from the “problems” caused by living in a hard-water area. But are they really necessary?
body: When water moves through soil and rocks, such as limestone, minerals dissolve into it and remain there when it comes out of your tap. These minerals are responsible for the limescale that builds up in your kettle.

“You know you’re living in a hard‑water area by how easy it is to lather up soap,” says Tobin. “If it is really difficult, and it forms a kind of scum rather than bubbles, you’re in a hard-water area. It’s healthy to drink, but it can trigger some issues.”

Washing your hair in hard water can leave mineral deposits on the hair shaft, which some believe make it look duller and feel rougher. There is evidence that calcium and magnesium can accumulate on hair washed in hard water, although the evidence that this causes damage is less clear.

Removing this buildup can cause problems, though, especially for those with dry or brittle hair. Tobin says the best shampoos for doing so are high lather and contain ingredients such as sulfates, which can be harsh on those hair types. “It’s this balancing act between removing the buildup and leaving enough oil in the system to condition the hair,” says Tobin.
points: Mineral deposits can accumulate, making hair drier, but removing them can cause different problems.
From hair treatments to shower filters, a wave of products have been launched promising to protect hair from the “problems” caused by living in a hard-water area.

articles.title: Going for gold: an early autumn road trip across Finland’s sparkling lake district
articles.summary: On a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green trees.
body: I wasn’t sure what to expect from an autumn trip to Finland, my first ever to the country, but spending an afternoon sprawled on a deck chair beneath blazing blue skies certainly wasn’t part of it. After a morning walking beneath the leafy canopy at the Mustila Arboretum – the oldest, most extensive botanical garden in the country – and a lunchtime wine-tasting (more of which later), my friend Sara and I pitched up at the Sahanlahti resort, deep in the Finnish Lakeland, only to find sun-drenched scenery that felt far more Mediterranean than Nordic.

Sahanlahti was the second stop on a mid-September road trip from Helsinki to the shores of Lake Saimaa; a journey in search of ruska, the spectacular autumn colours that blaze for a few short weeks before the long Finnish winter sets in. However, on our opening drive east from the airport to the Radalla resort, set on Lake Urajärvi, most of the thousands of trees we drove past were resolutely green, with just the very tips of the leaves tinged with auburn, like a foliage balayage.
points: On a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green trees.

articles.title: A new start after 60: I was always quiet – but at 82 I’m a famous, funny fashion influencer
articles.summary: Vivienne Truran was a civil servant and antiques dealer, who spent most of her life in the background. At 80, she realised how outgoing she was, and started a soaringly successful new career. ‘It took me till I was 80 to realise that I’m quite an outgoing and loud person,” says Vivienne Truran.
body: It all started 18 months ago. “I think I want to be an influencer,” she announced in one of her first reels. “Now, what can I influence people in?”

Wasn’t Truran outgoing when she was younger? “No,” she says. “My husband, Martin, was 6ft 4in. Rugby player, good-looking chap. When he walked into the room, he took the room. So I, like a good wife, was in the background. You can’t have two noisy people in a relationship. It doesn’t work.”

They were happily married for more than 40 years; but Martin got dementia and had a number of strokes, and died in hospital during Covid. Truran has no children, and no siblings. Feeling isolated, she would make a cake and sometimes take a piece to her then neighbour – now talent manager – James Rolling, and they became friends. It was Rolling who persuaded her to get in front of the camera.

He introduced her to his friends as his carer, for a joke; hence her Instagram tag @vivthecarer. They “respect each other and are a good team”, Truran says, but if she could change her tag, she would be “Viv from the Vale … like Jenny from the block”. She describes herself as a “timeless fashionista”, which she says is her third career.
points: Vivienne Truran was a civil servant and antiques dealer, who spent most of her life in the background.

articles.title: ‘Work hard – nobody cares how good you used to be’: Paul Smith at 80 on love, fun and his fabulous life in fashion
articles.summary: With the release of his new biography, the British designer talks about leaving school at 15, the real reason he won’t retire and why no one wears velvet trousers any more.
body: Sir Paul Smith has just turned 80 – and he has the enviable energy of someone more than half his age, swimming each day before 6am. He’s about to publish his memoir, Threads: My Life in Style. It’s been a good opportunity to do a stocktake. His has undoubtedly been a lucky life – right place, right time, right people (not least his wife, Pauline, whom he met at the age of 21 and who has been integral to his success) – but it’s also a story of hard work, integrity and modesty. We’ll get to whether those values are still relevant in a harsher, more competitive world, and whether Paul Smith can survive.
points: With the release of his new biography, the British designer talks about leaving school at 15, the real reason he won’t retire and why no one wears velvet trousers any more.

articles.title: 4 Key Takeaways From Tokyo Fashion Week SS27
articles.summary: With many emerging local designers showing outside of TFW, the SS27 schedule felt sparse. But this season, JFWO seized the opportunity to showcase international talent.
body: When you incubate and support local talent you hope will reach global relevance, how can you keep reaping the rewards?

That’s the question that Japan Fashion Week Organization (JFWO) is wrestling with this season, as Rakuten Fashion Week Tokyo evaluates its standing as a springboard for emerging designers — who are increasingly springing away. With many of its biggest names moving off schedule or showing abroad, the event must look elsewhere to maintain relevance.

The week nevertheless remains a reliable arena to scout for talent, as new designers enter the fashion week system through a combined effort of awards systems and a fresh international push. Here’s what you missed from the week.

There were 27 shows on the main schedule across six days, but many of Tokyo’s biggest domestic designers were absent, having either opted to showcase their collections via lookbook shoots or to hold off-schedule shows earlier in the season, usually in order to be closer to the men’s schedule or to the pre-summer buying season in Paris.

articles.title: 'The Gentlemen' Season 2 Takes Us From English Country Estates to Italian Palazzos in Mob Territory
articles.summary: From the rolling hills of Surrey to Italy's Lake Maggiore, these are the filming locations to look out for.
body: On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed?

The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire.

In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito).
points: From the rolling hills of Surrey to Italy's Lake Maggiore, these are the filming locations to look out for.

articles.title: The Story Behind Kendall Jenner’s Ultra-Rare, Artist-Made Earrings
articles.summary: Kendall Jenner looked to Peggy Guggenheim—Venice’s legendary adopted art-world grande dame—as inspiration for her first Venice Film Festival looks.
body: For all the dresses, diamonds, and dramatic water-taxi entrances that define the collective image of Venice Film Festival, one of Kendall Jenner’s most special accessories this week was a true “if you know you know” moment.

While in Venice for her first-ever turn on the storied Lido, Jenner stepped out in a smoke-gray, bell-sleeved, silky and sheer Vivienne Westwood dress, a woven Maison Ola basket bag, vintage Manolos (from her go-to, The Vintage Marché ), and a pair of abstract silver earrings. To the uninitiated eye, they were simply an elegant, slightly off-kilter addition to the look, fitting into Jenner’s pared back, The Row-forward aesthetic. But they are, truly, miniature works of art: a pair of Alexander Calder earrings dating to 1955, made from hammered silver and steel wire.

And they weren’t pulled from the archive of a major jewelry house; they came from Louisa Guinness, the London-based gallerist who has spent decades collecting, commissioning, and dealing in jewelry made by artists, from Calder and Man Ray to Niki De Saint Phalle and Anish Kapoor.
points: Kendall Jenner looked to Peggy Guggenheim—Venice’s legendary adopted art-world grande dame—as inspiration for her first Venice Film Festival looks.

articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers and Her Leg Hair Make for a Memorable Venice Film Festival Debut
articles.summary: For a turn around the Lido, musician and “Primetime” actor Phoebe Bridgers embraced the glamorous yet free-spirited Venice dress codes her way.
body: Yesterday, Phoebe Bridgers made her debut at the Venice Film Festival, where her first turn as an actor, in A24’s Primetime, was received with an enthusiastic seven-minute standing ovation and chants of “Phoebe! Phoebe!” The musician also brought a more unexpected detail to the Lido.

The singer arrived at the film’s photocall in a sharply tailored black skirt suit from Gucci’s fall 2026 collection. She accessorized with Gucci oval-frame sunglasses, Stuart Weitzman Babette pumps, and a chunky Leo Black Grandfather silver signet ring. With this sleek, controlled silhouette, her hair swept back and makeup kept soft and barely there, it was a look that reveled in the elegantly ladylike with a contemporary edge.

Her legs were left visibly unshaven beneath the abbreviated hemline—and rather than undermining the femininity of the look, unapologetic hair sharpened it. Bridgers’s multiple leg tattoos were also on show, including a tattoo of intertwined thorns and leaves and a black-ink rendering of a house that references her Punisher album.
points: For a turn around the Lido, musician and “Primetime” actor Phoebe Bridgers embraced the glamorous yet free-spirited Venice dress codes her way.

articles.title: Ever Anderson Marked Her First Venice Film Festival Premiere in Style
articles.summary: The rising actor and daughter of Milla Jovovich wore Dior and vintage for her first Venice: “I wanted something that was easy to wear but super fun and flashy.”
body: It was an exciting Venice Film Festival for rising actor Ever Anderson this year. The 18-year-old star—and daughter to Milla Jovovich—marked her first turn on the Lido this week with the premiere of her new film, Barthélemy Grossmann’s Father Joe, co-starring Kiefer Sutherland and Al Pacino. (Not a bad way to debut, alongside two such Hollywood heavyweights.) “It was just such an incredible project to work on,” says Anderson of her buzzy role.

The action-thriller film follows a man of faith (Sutherland) engaging in a violent war against Manhattan's criminal underworld; Anderson’s Felicity becomes his unlikely sidekick. “Her empathy and non-judgmental lens toward others was what drew me toward her,” says Anderson, who instantly resonated with the character. “She really felt like a real person when I read the script, which is rare, because normally a character doesn’t feel real on a page until a human plays them—but this wasn’t the case for Felicity. She was so well written that her spirit quite literally jumped off the page.”

articles.title: Vancouver’s Best Family-Friendly Hotels, From a Local Who Has Tried Them All
articles.summary: From mini robes to pizza-making classes, these Vancouver hotels make family stays fun for everyone.
body: As someone who was born and raised in Vancouver, I’ve seen the city through all stages of life: as a curious teen looking for adventure, as a single twenty-something eager for fun, as a new mom searching for ways to entertain my toddlers, and now as a mom of teens, helping them find new thrills in the city we call home. Regardless of which stage of life you're in, Vancity has something for everyone.

When I think of the best family-friendly hotels in Vancouver, I think of spots that make it easy to get around (even without a car) and that have room service or a restaurant with options for picky eaters. With three kids, I also always appreciate some extra space for everyone to settle down after a busy day of exploring. And if there’s a pool, my kids’ trip is pretty much made. For teens, the ability to roam freely on their own is another big perk, so I like a hotel that’s close to the action, with plenty to explore within walking distance.
The family-friendly hotels below put you in the heart of Vancouver, with plenty of kid-friendly perks that make it easy to settle in—and hard to leave.
